analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related limitations, like extra breaks, seating, or lifting limits.
analysis.headline: The bill won bipartisan support with 40 Senate cosponsors and cleared committee unanimously in effect, but sat on the Senate calendar for 15 months and never got a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers with 15 or more workers, and for government employers, to deny reasonable accommodations to workers limited by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, unless the accommodation is an undue hardship. That means things like more frequent bathroom breaks, a stool to sit on, limits on heavy lifting, or time off for doctor's appointments, rather than being forced onto unpaid leave. It also bars employers from forcing a pregnant worker onto leave when an accommodation would work, from retaliating against workers who ask, and from denying jobs because an accommodation is needed. Workers could sue, and states could not claim constitutional immunity from such lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant workers and applicants — including in physically demanding jobs like retail, warehousing, nursing, and manufacturing — who today often must choose between unpaid leave, risky work, or quitting. The bill gives them a legal right to modest, common-sense accommodations, with remedies including attorney's fees and damages, and applies the same protection to federal, state, and congressional employees.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must provide reasonable accommodations to known pregnancy-related limitations unless they can show the accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the business [S2].

Employers cannot force a pregnant worker to take paid or unpaid leave if another reasonable accommodation would work, cannot deny job opportunities because an accommodation is needed, and cannot punish a worker for requesting or using one [S2].

A worker can still be considered 'qualified' even if a temporary inability to do an essential function can be reasonably accommodated, so a short-term limitation does not cost the worker protection [S4].
Enforcement borrows the remedies of existing civil rights law, including compensatory damages and attorney's fees, and states are stripped of 11th Amendment immunity so state employees can sue [S2].
The bill protects workers from retaliation and coercion for exercising these rights, and requires the EEOC to issue regulations within two years with concrete examples of accommodations [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees and government employers bear the cost of providing accommodations — chairs, schedules, light duty, temporary reassignments — plus compliance and potential litigation exposure. States lose their immunity from lawsuits by state employees. The bill explicitly does not require employer health plans to cover any particular treatment, so insurers and health plans bear no coverage cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Larger employers, state governments, insurers spared

drawbacks.text: Employers would face new compliance obligations and lawsuit exposure, and even the bill's supporters acknowledged this by including a provision that blocks damages awards when an employer shows it made good-faith efforts to find an accommodation with the worker [S4].

The 15-employee coverage threshold mirrors the existing civil rights floor, so workers at very small employers get no help, and the bill does not guarantee any paid leave — it only prevents leave from being forced when an accommodation exists [S2].

The 'undue hardship' standard is borrowed from disability law, which in practice lets employers defend denial of accommodations in court, so enforcement depends on workers being able to bring claims [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accommodations at issue — stools, water breaks, lifting limits, schedule tweaks — are typically low-cost, and the undue-hardship escape plus the good-faith damages shield narrow the burden on employers. The main gap is coverage: 15-employee threshold aside, the bill relies on individual enforcement rather than any guarantee of leave or pay, so its protection is only as strong as a worker's ability to file a claim. On balance the costs to employers are modest against a real gain in job security for hundreds of thousands of pregnant workers a year.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate HELP committee reported it favorably and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote, and the Congress ended with it still waiting.

narrative.text: Introduced April 29, 2021 by Senator Casey with an ideologically mixed group of original cosponsors including Republicans Cassidy, Capito, Murkowski, and Grassley [S1].
The Senate HELP committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on August 3, 2021, and Senator Murray reported it on September 30, 2021 [S6].
On September 30, 2021 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 141, meaning it was waiting for floor time [S6].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a Senate floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and state governments are better off because the bill died: they avoid a new accommodation mandate, the associated litigation exposure, and the waiver of state sovereign immunity. Pregnant workers gained no federal right to accommodation from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled bipartisan original cosponsors including Grassley, Cassidy, Capito, and Murkowski

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably from committee with an amendment and moved it to the Senate calendar

for.name: 40 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including 32 of 48 Senate Democrats, 7 of 50 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan support before the floor

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote despite it sitting on the legislative calendar for over a year with bipartisan backing

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines: of 40 cosponsors, 32 were Democrats, 7 were Republicans, and 1 was an Independent, and the bill cleared the HELP committee with no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (retail, warehousing, healthcare, manufacturing, hospitality)
industries.note: The bill would require these employers to provide pregnancy accommodations or prove undue hardship, and exposes them to damages suits with attorney's fees. The good-faith limit on damages softens litigation exposure. Their cost is the accommodation workers gain.

The bill expressly waives state 11th Amendment immunity, so state employees could sue their employers for denial of pregnancy accommodations. This was a notable expansion of worker rights against government employers.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer-sponsored health plans
industries.note: The bill explicitly states it cannot require any employer-sponsored health plan to cover any particular item, procedure, or treatment, so plans and insurers face no new coverage mandate. This leaves coverage questions to other laws.
